Overview:
This document contains capability definitions for the DevSecOps Capability Assessment Model project capabilities.

It is not the intent of this document to be a comprehensive reference on all aspects of Agile and Dev(Sec)Ops frameworks and modern software engineering.  The description in each section is just a summary of what the team and organization should be capable of; the references provide a more in-depth review of the area and should be consulted when developing an improvement plan.
Terms and Definitions: Backup
The storage of all information needed to restore the system should the original be compromised in some way. It is also the process by which this information is stored
Continuous Integration (CI)
the practice of regularly merging completed work on a mainline branch; and building, scanning, and testing the merged work when it is merged
Customer
A person or organization who requested the product or service the team is delivering. The customer’s needs and priorities guide what the team builds.
Deliver
Make the release available to external customers
Deploy
Install the system into a production environment
Install
Install the system into any target environment
Integration Test

A test that tests a set of functions or modules working together, typically by accessing an API. A system test may depend on external resources, but these dependencies should be minimized and well-defined
Pipeline
A collection of automated tools which build and inspect source code to create a release and prepare it for delivery and deployment
Promotion
The process, whether automated or manual, of approving that the system moves from one environment to another. For example: “the system was promoted from development to test”
Recovery
The process of using a backup to restore system functionality
Regression Test
Any test that is run regularly to ensure the system has not regressed, i.e., that existing functionality is not broken
Release
A package containing the deployable artifacts and related documentation that is delivered to the customer for deployment
Stakeholder

Anyone outside of the team who has a vested interest in the team’s output.  While customers are the most obvious stakeholders, stakeholders can also include internal or external groups who are interested in the output as an input to their work (e.g., a Security team that must review the product before it is released, end users).
System Test

A test that runs against a fully- or partially-deployed application, using the external interfaces of the application. Where the application is split into microservices, each microservice can have its own set of system tests, and the overall application could also have system tests
Team

A small, self-organizing group focused on collaboration, customer feedback, and adaptation to change that owns that owns delivering and operating a product or service.  In early phases, a team includes developers and a manager and, as it matures, incorporates testing, operations, and security roles to support full DevSecOps practices.
Unit Test

A a small, fast test that exercises one function or module in the codebase. A unit test will typically stub out any internal or external dependencies, in particular there should not be dependencies on any resources outside the immediate environment, specifically the source code base and the build environment
Work Item

Identifies work to be done by the project team. The work item can identify several different types of work, for example a bugfix, a feature to be implemented, or a process improvement. Also commonly known as: issue, story, task, ticket, feature
Acronyms: National Institute of Standards and Technology

Roles.{id: R1} Automation Engineer: Owns the scripts that run on the pipeline, including the top-level pipeline definition file, normally stored in version control in e.g., .github/builds/build.yml.  Owns any project-specific or project-owned tools used by the pipeline.
Roles.{id: R2} Pipeline Infrastructure Enginee: Owns the framework and infrastructure that supports running the pipeline.  This role may support a shared environment used by different projects, including tools (build orchestrators, scanners, test frameworks, etc.) that are made available to the different projects.
Roles.{id: R3} Software Developer: Writes code or implements application changes via other means (e.g., no-code, low-code, xml, yaml) in response to customer requests, bugs, and security needs. This code may be built, tested, and deployed via the pipeline.
Roles.{id: R4} Scrum Master: Provides guidance and support for the team’s agile methodology. Focuses on eliminating roadblocks and encouraging the team’s agile work.
Roles.{id: R5} Software Tester: Develops and runs tests on developed code and product functionality to ensure requirements are met and bugs have not been created.
Roles.{id: R6} Release Manager: Schedules, coordinates, and manages releases of the application.  Works with the customer and the team to set expectations for each release.  Ensures release procedures are established and followed.
Roles.{id: R7} Cloud Engineer: Manages cloud infrastructure (e.g., creation, maintenance, monitoring) for all environments (e.g., development, test, production).
Roles.{id: R8} Security: Assesses and contributes to security aspects of the product, including all environments (e.g., development, test, production).  Responsible for putting in place measures and practices to support Authority to Operate (ATO) or continuous Authority to Operate (cATO).  May include the roles of Security Controls Assessor (SCA), Vulnerability Assessment Team (VAT), Information System Security Officer (ISSO), and Security Architect.
Roles.{id: R9} Operations: Responsible for all aspects of the application running in production, including supporting infrastructure, security, monitoring, and application performance/functionality.
Roles.{id: R10} Product Owner: Acts as a representative of the customer. As such, they define stories and prioritize the product backlog in partnership with both the customer and team to ensure the timely delivery of value.  They may have responsibilities outside of their team, including working with program management, security (e.g., ISSO), and other stakeholders.
